# Conda and containers without wrecking your home directory {#sec-conda}

::: {.tldr}
Conda is supported, but its default is to dump gigabytes into your 50 GB home directory —
which will fill it and break things. **Redirect conda's package cache and environments into
`/project/<proj>/software` before you create anything.** For reproducible, portable software
(especially things that are painful to build), use **Apptainer** containers instead.
:::

## Conda: great, but point it away from home first

The `miniconda3` module gives you conda:

```bash
module load miniconda3/24.3.0
```

By default, conda writes environments and a package cache into `~/.conda` and
`~/miniconda3` — i.e. straight into your **50 GB home quota**. A couple of scientific
environments will fill it. Fix this **once, before creating any environments**, by telling
conda to live in your project's 250 GB software space.

Create `~/.condarc`:

```yaml
pkgs_dirs:
  - /project/cowy-firesurro/software/<you>/conda/pkgs
envs_dirs:
  - /project/cowy-firesurro/software/<you>/conda/envs
```

Now new environments and the download cache land in project space:

```bash
conda create -n fire python=3.12 numpy xarray netcdf4
conda activate fire
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Do this before your first `conda create`
If you create environments first and *then* set `.condarc`, the old ones are stranded in
home and you'll wonder why home is still full. Set `.condarc` on day one. If you've already
made the mess: `conda env list`, remove the home-based envs, and recreate them under project
space.
:::

Other conda notes:

- **No `mamba`** is installed anywhere on the cluster — use `conda` directly. (Recent conda
  is much faster than it used to be, so this is less painful than it once was.)
- Activate conda **inside your submit script**, not just interactively, so batch jobs get the
  same environment (@sec-anatomy).
- `conda clean -a` reclaims space from the package cache periodically.

## Apptainer: containers for reproducibility and portability

A **container** bundles an application with its entire operating-system environment into a
single image file. On HPC the runtime is **Apptainer** (formerly Singularity) — it runs
containers as *you*, with no root, which is why it's the HPC-safe alternative to Docker.

```bash
module load apptainer/1.4.1

# Pull a Docker image and convert it to an Apptainer image (.sif):
apptainer pull mytool.sif docker://ghcr.io/someorg/mytool:latest

# Run something inside it:
apptainer exec mytool.sif mytool --help

# Bind your data into the container so it can see it:
apptainer exec --bind /project/cowy-firesurro:/data mytool.sif mytool /data/input.nc
```

Store `.sif` images in `/project/<proj>/software` — they can be large.

### When to reach for a container vs. a module vs. conda

| Situation | Best choice |
|---|---|
| The software is already an Lmod module | **module** (@sec-modules) — least effort |
| Pure Python/R stack, you want to iterate | **conda** |
| Complex native dependencies that fight the system | **Apptainer** |
| You need bit-for-bit reproducibility across machines | **Apptainer** |
| A published tool ships a Docker image | **Apptainer** (`apptainer pull docker://…`) |

::: {.callout-note}
## GPUs inside containers
To use the node's GPUs from inside a container, add the `--nv` flag so Apptainer exposes the
NVIDIA driver: `apptainer exec --nv mytool.sif ...`. Pair this with a GPU job (@sec-gpu).
:::

With software sorted, we reach the heart of the book: getting the scheduler to run your work
(Part V, starting at @sec-why-scheduler).
